slides.title: Loops
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter teaches repetition: while, for and range, the containers a loop visits, modules and leaving a program early. The same examples run on the chapter page.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: while loops, for and range, what a for loop visits, modules and leaving early, and two short programs.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. What decides when a loop repeats and when it stops? And which parts of the book differ in current Python? The answers come back in the summary.

slides.title: Part 1: Repeating with while
slides.say: Part one. A while loop tests first, then runs its block. Watch the test turn False. Break and continue change the flow, and the walrus names a value inside the test.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: repeating
slides.say: A washing machine repeats a cycle until the programme ends. A guard decides at every round whether to walk another one.

slides.title: while: repeat as long as the test is true
slides.say: The test comes first. Run the block, come back, test again. The last test is False, so the block is skipped.

slides.title: An accumulator adds up 1 to 100
slides.say: An accumulator starts at zero and collects. The chart shows the running total at every twentieth number. Gauss's formula gives the same 5050 without a loop.

slides.title: Story: Gauss added 1 to 100 without a loop
slides.say: The Gauss tale has a paper trail back to an 1856 memorial, so call it a legend. The loop and the formula both give 5050.

slides.title: while True runs until break leaves it
slides.say: While True never stops by itself, so break is its exit. The iterator replaces a typing person, so the example runs without a keyboard. Count the passes.

slides.title: continue skips the rest of one pass
slides.say: Continue does not leave the loop; it returns to the test. Even numbers skip the append. Compare the two lists with the picture of the numbers 1 to 8.

slides.title: The assignment expression in a loop test
slides.say: The walrus reads and names in one expression, which is what the PEP's own file-reading loop needs. The empty string at the end is False, so the loop stops.

slides.title: Story: the walrus operator and PEP 572
slides.say: PEP 572 was created in February 2018 and shipped in Python 3.8. Guido stepped down as BDFL on 12 July 2018.

slides.title: Part 2: Counting with for and range
slides.say: Part two. For takes the items of a sequence one by one. Range describes numbers without storing them, and it stops before the stop value.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: for and range
slides.say: The postman has a list and visits each house. Range is the list of house numbers, printed on demand. A school year shows why a half-open interval has no overlaps.

slides.title: for: one value of range(5) per pass
slides.say: For needs no counter. The chart shows the total after each pass. After the loop, i still holds 4, because the loop variable is never deleted.

slides.title: range(start, stop, step)
slides.say: Start is included, stop is not. Length is stop minus start. A negative step counts down. Two neighbouring ranges leave no gap and no overlap.

slides.title: Story: why range stops before the end
slides.say: Dijkstra's memo EWD831 is dated 11 August 1982. Half-open ranges give lengths as stop minus start and let neighbours meet.

slides.title: range describes numbers; it does not store them
slides.say: Range stores three numbers and computes the rest on demand. That is why a range of a billion costs nothing. Slicing gives another range.

slides.title: Part 3: What a for loop visits
slides.say: Part three. A loop can visit lists, tuples, dictionaries and strings. Enumerate and zip remove index arithmetic. Under every for sit iter and next.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: what a loop visits
slides.say: A list changes, a tuple does not, a dictionary looks up by key. Unpacking puts each part of a pair into its own name. The walrus names a value and uses it in one move.

slides.title: for visits a list and a tuple
slides.say: Both containers are visited in order. The chart shows the length of each pet name. The tuple cannot be changed; the list can.

slides.title: for visits the pairs of a dictionary
slides.say: Items gives pairs, and the loop unpacks each into two names. Values gives the values only. The chart shows the three ages.

slides.title: enumerate and zip replace index arithmetic
slides.say: Enumerate gives counter and item. Zip gives pairs from two lists. Both remove range(len(...)). The chart shows the scores.

slides.title: zip: stop silently, or insist on equal lengths
slides.say: Without strict, zip drops the extra item silently. With strict it raises a ValueError. This check arrived in Python 3.10.

slides.title: Under every for: iter and next
slides.say: A for loop asks for an iterator, then calls next until StopIteration. The diagram shows the two steps. An iterator returns itself; a list does not.

slides.title: break, and the else clause of a loop
slides.say: The else of a loop runs when no break happened. The first list has an even number, so break fires and else is skipped. The second list has none.

slides.title: Part 4: Modules and leaving early
slides.say: Part four. Import opens a module and keeps its names in a namespace. Sys.exit ends a program by raising an exception that carries the exit status.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: modules
slides.say: A module is a toolbox with a label. A namespace keeps its names apart from yours. If no shop on the search path has the toolbox, Python says so.

slides.title: import random: a seeded dice roll
slides.say: The seed fixes the sequence, so everyone sees the same six rolls. The chart counts how often each face came up. A module is an object with a name.

slides.title: Two import forms, two namespaces
slides.say: Two ways in. Import math keeps the module name; from-import copies one name. The diagram shows the two namespaces. Sqrt alone is not defined.

slides.title: When import fails: the module search path
slides.say: The search path is just a list of folders; the first line shows it. Python visits each folder in turn. Nothing is found, so ModuleNotFoundError names the module.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: leaving early
slides.say: Sys.exit is the stop button; the exit status tells the caller why. An exception interrupts normal flow. The warning sign is the new Python 3.14 check on finally.

slides.title: sys.exit() ends a program with an exit status
slides.say: Sys.exit raises SystemExit, so except and finally both see it. The exit status is 3 here; zero means success. The line after sys.exit never runs.

slides.title: Part 5: Two short programs
slides.say: Part five. Two short programs from the book, with scripted input so they run on the page. Predict the output, then check it against the run.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: short programs
slides.say: Both programs are small games with a loop of turns. The summary and the practice questions close the chapter.

slides.title: Guess the Number: at most six guesses
slides.say: The secret is 11. The scripted guesses walk toward it: 10 is low, 15 is high, 12 is high, 11 is right. Break leaves the loop; taken keeps the count.

slides.title: Guess the Number: the ending, with for and else
slides.say: The else on the inner loop is the lose branch. It runs only if break never happened. The chart shows how many guesses each game used.

slides.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors: one round
slides.say: Three outcomes, one chain of tests. The diagram shows the two moves and the result. Paper covers rock, so the player wins.

slides.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors: six rounds and a score
slides.say: Six rounds, one accumulator for each outcome. The chart is the final score: two wins, two losses, two ties.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. The walrus came in 3.8, strict zip in 3.10. Python 3.14 warns about return, break or continue that leave a finally block. Control-C stops an endless loop.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the loop statements and tools of this chapter by what they do.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run them on the chapter page.
